Our blissful union with you, who are so full of love, is right now!" What is this, mother! He is grabbing my hand! What is this, mother!
commentary: Sincere love and devotion are the keys that unlock divine union. God does not approach the hearts of those who are insincere or unready. For the soul who sings with love of the Meyppōtha Maṉṟam (Hall of True Knowledge), however, God rushes to unite. The message is one of warm encouragement: genuine love dissolves all sense of delay, making blissful union possible "right now."

translit: meykkulam pōṟṟa viḷaṅku maṇāḷar vittakar ampalam mēvum aḻakar ikkula mātarum yāṉumeṉ nātar iṉṉaruḷ āṭalkaḷ paṉṉuṟum pōtu poykkulam pēcip pulampātē peṇṇē pūraṇa nōkkam poruntiṉai nītāṉ ekkulam eṉkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā eṉkai piṭikkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā.
translation: He is the Bridegroom praised by the people of truth, the Wise One, the Beautiful One who dwells in the Ambalam. While these ladies of our circle and I were describing the sweet, graceful plays of my Lord, He said, "Woman, do not lament, speaking of false caste. You yourself have attained the perfect vision." What is this, mother, He asks, "What caste?" What is this, mother, He grasps my hand.
commentary: Vallalar calls caste false: poykkulam, 'false caste.' When the soul has attained the perfect vision, God dismisses the question of birth-group outright: "What caste?" Caste was never true. The only identity that matters is the soul's direct relationship with God.

translit: vemmata neñciṭai mēvuṟa uṉṉār vempala māṟṟumeṉ ampala vāṇar cammata māmaṭa vārkaḷum nāṉum tattuvam pēcikkoṇ ṭottuṟum pōtu immatam pēci iṟaṅkātē peṇṇē ēkaci vōkattai eytiṉai nītāṉ emmatam eṉkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā eṉkai piṭikkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā.
translation: He does not think to dwell in hearts ruled by fierce religious zeal; He is my Lord of the Ambalam who removes the burning fruits of karma. While the agreeable ladies and I were harmoniously discussing the tattvas, He said, "Woman, do not lower yourself by speaking of 'this religion.' You yourself have attained the state of oneness with Sivam." What is this, mother, He asks, "What religion?" What is this, mother, He grasps my hand.
commentary: God is not confined to any single religion or set of beliefs. The soul, still caught up in philosophical discussions, is told that her attachment to "this religion" is a distraction. Having attained the state of being one with Sivam, the ultimate Reality, she has moved beyond all dogma. God’s question, "What religion?", shows that from the divine perspective, these human-made divisions are irrelevant.

translit: pāroṭu viṇṇum paṭaittapaṇ pāḷar paṟṟam palattārcol ciṟṟam palattār vāriṭu koṅkaiyar maṅkaiya rōṭē maṉṟakam pāṭi makiḻkiṉṟa pōtu ēruṭam poṉṟeṉa eṇṇēlnī peṇṉē emmuṭam puṉṉaiiṇaintiṅ kemakkē īruṭam peṉkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā eṉkai piṭikkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā.
translation: He is the benevolent One who created earth and sky, the One of the Chitrambalam, praised by those whose refuge is the Ambalam. While I was with the women with tightly-bound breasts, singing joyfully of the sacred hall, He said, "Woman, do not think your beautiful body is only one. My body has joined with you here, so for Us there are now two bodies." What is this, mother! He grasps my hand, what is this, mother!
commentary: Union transforms the body itself. God tells the soul not to think her beautiful body is hers alone: His body has joined with her, so that He now has two bodies, His own and hers. Her body has become God's own body. This is the bodily union Vallalar speaks of throughout the Sixth Thirumurai, not a figure of speech.

translit: maṟappaṟṟa neñciṭai vāḻkiṉṟa vaḷḷal malappaṟ ṟaṟuttavar vāḻttu maṇāḷar ciṟappuṟṟa maṅkaiyar tammoṭu nāṉtāṉ ciṟṟam palampāṭic celkiṉṟa pōtu puṟappaṟ ṟakaṟṟat toṭaṅkātē peṇṇē pulaiakap paṟṟai aṟuttāy niṉakkē iṟappaṟṟa teṉkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā eṉkai piṭikkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā.
translation: He is the Benefactor who lives in hearts free from forgetfulness, the Bridegroom praised by those who have severed their attachment to impurity. While I was walking with the distinguished ladies, singing of the Chitrambalam, He said, "Woman, do not even begin to remove external attachments. You have already cut the vile inner attachment; for you, there is no more death." What is this, mother! He grasps my hand, what is this, mother!
commentary: True liberation is an inside job. The soul is advised to stop focusing on removing external attachments, because the real victory has already been won: cutting the "vile inner attachment," the fundamental impurity that binds the soul. Once this root cause of bondage is gone, the consequence is freedom from death itself.

translit: āṟeṉum antaṅkaḷ ākiaṉ ṟākum ampalat tāṭalcey āṉanta cittar tēṟaṟi vākic civāṉu pavattē ciṉmaya māynāṉ tiḷaikkiṉṟa pōtu māṟakal vāḻviṉil vāḻkiṉṟa peṇṇē vallavaḷ nīyēim mānilai mēlē ēṟiṉai eṉkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā eṉkai piṭikkiṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā.
translation: He is the blissful Siddha who dances in the Hall, becoming the six ends and remaining beyond them. When I was rejoicing as pure consciousness and becoming clear knowledge in the experience of Siva, he said to me, "O woman living a life free of conflict! You are the capable one, and you have ascended to this great state." He says this, mother, and he holds my hand. What is this, mother?
commentary: This verse describes the devotee's own ascent into a state of divine consciousness. She is no longer just a worshipper, but is herself immersed in the direct experience of God (Sivānubhavam), abiding as pure consciousness (cinmayam). God, appearing as the blissful master of reality (Ānanda Siddhar), confirms her achievement, acknowledging that she has reached a supreme and unshakeable state of being.
NOTES
Note 365

translit: aṉṉaippārppāl - ā. pā. patippu.
translation: aṉṉaippārppāl — reading of the Ā. Pā. edition.
Note 366

translit: emmuṭam pummai - ā. pā. patippu.,
translation: emmuṭam pummai — reading of the Ā. Pā. Edition.

translit: paruvamilāk kuṟaiyālō pakutivakai yālō paḻakkamilā maiyiṉālō paṭiṟṟuviṉai yālō iruvakaimā yaiyiṉālō āṇavatti ṉālō eṉṉālō piṟarālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ caruvaloḻin teṉmaṉamām pāṅkipakai yāṉāḷ taṉittaparai eṉumvaḷartta tāyummukam pārāḷ niruvamaṭap peṇkaḷelām valatukoḻik kiṉṟār nipuṇareṅkaḷ naṭarāyar niṉaivaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because of some flaw in my maturity, or some fundamental defect? Is it from lack of experience, or from deceitful karma? Is it due to the two kinds of illusion, or because of ego? Is it my fault, or someone else's? I do not know the reason. My friend, who is my own mind, has abandoned affection and become my enemy. The mother who raised me, the transcendent Parai, will not look at my face. All the other peerless women are spreading cruel rumors. I do not know the mind of our expert Lord, Natarāyar.
commentary: The devotee feels utterly abandoned by God and is searching for a reason. She runs through a list of possible spiritual failings: her own immaturity, past actions (karma), illusion (māyai), and ego (āṇavam). In this state of despair, her own mind turns against her, and even the Divine Mother (Parai, the Supreme Power) feels distant. It's a powerful depiction of the "dark night of the soul," a period of intense doubt and loneliness on the path to God.

translit: ampalattē tirunaṭañcey aṭimalareṉ muṭimēl aṇintiṭamuṉ cilacoṉṉēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi empalattē emmiṟaivaṉ eṉṉaimaṇam purivāṉ eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ vampicaittēṉ eṉaeṉatu pāṅkipakai yāṉāḷ vaḷartteṭutta taṉittāyum malarntumukam pārāḷ nimpamarak kaṉiyāṉār maṟṟaiyarkaḷ ellām nipuṇareṅkaḷ naṭarāyar niṉaivaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I spoke earlier of placing on my head the flower-like feet of the One who dances in the sacred hall? Or is it because I said, "My Lord will marry me in our own hall"? Is it for this reason? I do not know why. Saying I was making empty boasts, my friend has become my enemy. The unique mother who raised me no longer looks at my face with a smile. All the others have become as bitter as neem fruit. I do not know the thoughts of our expert Lord, Natarāyar.
commentary: The devotee wonders if her confidence in God's love has brought on this suffering. Her bold, public declarations of her relationship with the Lord (Natarāyar, the cosmic dancer) are seen as empty boasts by others, leading to her complete isolation. The spiritual path often brings misunderstanding from the world, and her certainty has made her a stranger.

translit: kaṇṇuṟaṅkēṉ uṟaṅkiṉumeṉ kaṇavaroṭu kalakkum kaṉavaṉṟi ilaieṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi eṇṇuṟaṅkā nilavilavar irukkumiṭam pukuvēṉ eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ peṇṇaṭaṅkāḷ eṉattōḻi pēcimukaṅ kaṭuttāḷ peruntayavāl vaḷarttavaḷum varuntayalāḷ āṉāḷ maṇṇaṭaṅkāp paḻikūṟi maṟṟavarkaḷ iruntār vaḷḷalnaṭa rāyartiru vuḷḷamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, "I do not sleep, and even when I do, I have no dreams other than uniting with my Husband"? Or is it because I declared, "I will go to His dwelling in the mind-stopping moonlight"? Is it for this reason? I do not know why. "This woman is uncontrollable," my friend said, her face hardening. The one who raised me with great compassion has become a sorrowful stranger. The others linger, heaping on slanders too great for the earth to bear. I do not know the sacred will of the generous Lord Natarāyar.
commentary: Her total, uncompromising devotion to God is seen by others as scandalous. Because her entire life, sleeping and waking, revolves around uniting with her divine "Husband," she is considered wild and uncontrollable by worldly standards. This verse shows the deep conflict between social norms and the all-consuming nature of a true spiritual calling.

translit: ellāñcey vallaturai eṉkaṇavar eṉṟāl eṉakkumoṉṟu niṉakkumoṉṟā eṉṟaata ṉālō illāmai eṉakkillai ellārkkun taruvēṉ eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ kallārpōl eṉṉaimukam kaṭuttuniṉṟāḷ pāṅki kaḷitteṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum kalantaṉaḷaṅ kuṭaṉē cellāmai cilapukaṉṟu cirikkiṉṟār maṭavār cittarnaṭa rāyartiruc cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because, when I said "The Lord who can do anything is my Husband," I then asked "Is there one rule for me and another for you?" Or is it because I declared, "I know no lack; I will give to everyone"? Is it for this reason? I do not know why. My friend stood scowling at me like an uncultured person. The one who joyfully raised me immediately sided with her. The other women laugh, pointing out my improprieties. I do not know the sacred mind of the Siddha, Lord Natarāyar.
commentary: Through her connection to God, the "Lord who can do anything," the speaker feels a spiritual abundance that she wishes to share with all. Her declaration, "I know no lack; I will give to everyone," flows from this newfound divine empowerment. However, those around her hear this as an outrageous and improper claim to a status she doesn't possess, highlighting the conflict between the spiritual logic of grace and the world's logic of hierarchy.

translit: iccaielām vallaturai eṉṉaimaṇam purintār ēṭieṉak kiṇaievarkaḷ eṉṟaata ṉālō eccamayat tēvaraiyum iṉimatikka māṭṭēṉ eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ naccumarak kaṉipōlē pāṅkimaṉaṅ kacantāḷ nayanteṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum kayanteṭuppup pukaṉṟāḷ accamilāḷ ivaḷeṉṟē alaruraittār maṭavār aṇṇalnaṭa rāyartiru eṇṇamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because, after saying "The Lord who can fulfill all desires has married me," I asked, "O friend, who is my equal now?" Or is it because I announced, "Henceforth, I will not esteem the gods of any religion"? Is it for this reason? I do not know why. My friend's heart turned bitter, like the fruit of a poison tree. The one who raised me with love spoke mean and degrading words. "She is shameless!" the other women gossiped. I do not know the sacred intention of the great Lord Natarāyar.
commentary: For the soul that has experienced union with the ultimate Lord, all lesser gods and religious forms become secondary. When the speaker declares she will no longer respect other deities, she is expressing a profound shift in her spiritual reality. To her community, this sounds like blasphemy and shameless pride, earning her scorn and condemnation. Her singular focus on the highest truth alienates her from those who still adhere to conventional religious boundaries.

translit: vañcamilāt talaivarukkē mālaiyiṭṭēṉ ellā vāḻvumeṉṟaṉ vāḻveṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi eñcaluṟēṉ maṟṟavarpōl iṟantupiṟan tuḻalēṉ eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ añcumukaṅ kāṭṭiniṉṟāḷ pāṅkieṉai vaḷartta aṉṉaiyumap paṭiyāki eṉṉaimukam pārāḷ neñcuratta peṇkaḷelām nīṭṭinakaik kiṉṟār niruttarnaṭa rāyartiruk karuttaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I garlanded the guileless Lord and declared that all life is my life. Is it for that reason, or because I said, "Unlike others, I will not languish, dying and being reborn"? I do not know why. My confidante shows a frightened face; the mother who raised me is the same and will not look at me. All the hard-hearted women are pointing and laughing. I do not understand the sacred intention of the Dancer, the King of Dance.
commentary: The speaker voices two of the highest spiritual truths: that she is liberated from the cycle of death and rebirth, and that "all life is my life." This second phrase expresses the core principle of Anma Neya Orumaipadu (the unity of all souls). These are not abstract beliefs for her but experienced realities. To those still bound by ordinary consciousness, such statements are so far beyond the norm that they inspire fear and mockery.

translit: aṉṉamuṇa aḻaittaṉarnāṉ āṭummala raṭittēṉ aruntukiṉṟēṉ eṉa:uraittēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi eṉṉuyirnā yakaṉoṭunāṉ aṇaiyumiṭam eṅkē eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ tuṉṉuneṟik korutuṇaiyām tōḻimaṉaṅ kacantāḷ tuṇinteṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum cōrntamukam āṉāḷ neṉṉalotta peṇkaḷelāṅ kūṭinakaik kiṉṟār nipuṇareṅkaḷ naṭarāyar niṉaivaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: They called me to eat, but I swore upon his dancing, flower-like feet and said, "I am already partaking." They called me to eat, but I said, "I am drinking the honey of His dancing flower-feet." Is it because of that, or because I asked, "Where is the place I will unite with the Lord of my life?" I do not know the reason. I do not know the reason. My confidante, my companion on this dense path, has become bitter of heart. The one who resolved to raise me now has a weary face. All the women of yesterday’s ways gather and laugh. I do not know the mind of our expert, the King of Dance.
commentary: Devotion itself has become a source of nourishment that makes physical food seem irrelevant. The speaker's claim that she is "already partaking" by remembering the Lord's dancing feet shows she is sustained by a divine energy. This rejection of a basic human need for a mystical experience is incomprehensible to her family, who see only a wearying and strange obsession. The women of "yesterday's ways" represent a world unable to understand a life fed by God alone.

translit: potunaṭañcey turaimukattē taḷataḷaeṉ ṟoḷirum puṉṉakaieṉ poruḷeṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi ituvaraiyum varakkāṇēṉ taṭaiceytār evarō eṉappukaṉṟēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ putumukaṅkoṇ ṭeṉatutaṉit tōḻimaṉan tirintāḷ purinteṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum putumaicila pukaṉṟāḷ matuvukantu kaḷittavarpōl peṇkaḷnoṭik kiṉṟār vaḷḷalnaṭa rāyartiru vuḷḷamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I said, "The dazzlingly bright smile on the face of him who performs the universal dance is my property." Is it for that reason, or because I exclaimed, "I have not seen him arrive yet, who has obstructed him?" I do not know why. My only confidante’s mind has turned, her face now a strange mask. The one who lovingly raised me spoke some bizarre things. The women snap their fingers in derision, like people drunk on liquor. I do not know the sacred will of the generous King of Dance.
commentary: The speaker's intimacy with God is expressed in ways that sound shockingly presumptuous to others. To claim God's smile as her personal "property" is, for her, a statement of love's deep connection, but for the world, it is an act of supreme arrogance. Her impatience, crying out for God to appear, is the authentic cry of a soul in waiting, yet those around her see only erratic behavior, confirming their view that she has lost her mind.

translit: kaṇkalanta kaḷvareṉṉaik kaikalanta taruṇam karaṇamaṟin tilaṉeṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi eṇkalanta pōkamelām civapōkan taṉilē iruntateṉṟēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ viṇkalanta matimukantāṉ vēṟupaṭṭāḷ pāṅki viyanteṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum vēṟucila pukaṉṟāḷ paṇkalanta moḻimaṭavār paḻikūṟa lāṉār pattarpukaḻ naṭarāyar cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I said, "At the moment that thief whose eyes met mine embraced me, I lost awareness of my inner faculties." Is it for that reason, or because I said, "All the countless pleasures one can imagine are found within the bliss of Siva"? I do not know why. The face of my confidante, once like the sky-bound moon, has changed completely. The one who raised me with admiration spoke other, different words. The young women, whose words are like music, have started to blame me. I do not know the mind of the King of Dance, whom devotees praise.
commentary: This verse describes the state of mystical union where the individual self dissolves. When the speaker says she lost awareness of her "inner faculties" (karaṇam), she is referring to the ecstatic moment when mind, intellect, and ego merge into the divine. To an outsider, this experience looks like a loss of consciousness or sanity. Her declaration that all worldly pleasures are contained within this single bliss further marks her as someone who has abandoned the world's values, earning her blame.

translit: māṭamicai ōṅkunilā maṇṭapattē makiḻntēṉ vaḷḷaloṭu nāṉeṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi īṭaṟiyāc cukampukala eṉṉālē muṭiyā teṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ ēṭaviḻpūṅ kuḻaṟkōtait tōḻumukam pularntāḷ eṉaieṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum irakkamilāḷ āṉāḷ nāṭaṟiyap peṇkaḷelāṅ kūṭinakaik kiṉṟār nallanaṭa rāyarkarut tellaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I said, "I rejoiced with the generous Lord in the high, moonlit hall on the mansion's roof." Is it for that reason, or because I declared, "It is impossible for me to speak of this unequaled bliss"? I do not know why. The face of my confidante, a lady whose hair is adorned with unfurling flowers, has faded. The one who raised me has become merciless. All the women have gathered to laugh for the whole country to see. I do not know the bounds of the good King of Dance's intention.
commentary: The speaker's isolation becomes a public spectacle. Her attempt to convey the bliss of her union with God fails because the experience is beyond words. This inability to explain herself is taken as further proof of delusion. The reactions of those around her have hardened: her friend's face is "faded" with worry, and her mother's love has turned "merciless." The private struggle of the soul has now become a source of public humiliation.

translit: kaṟpūram maṇakkiṉṟa teṉmēṉi muḻutum kaṇavarmaṇam atuveṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi iṟpūvai aṟiyumaṭi naṭantavaṇṇam ellām eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ poṟpūviṉ mukamviyarttāḷ pāṅkiava ḷuṭaṉē purinteṭuttu vaḷarttavaḷum karintamukam paṭaittāḷ coṟpūvait toṭukkiṉṟār kālkaḷkaḷai yātē tuṉṉunaṭa rāyarkarut tellaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I said the camphor fragrance pervading his southern form was my husband's scent. Is it because of that? I said, "The fragrance of camphor fills my whole body; it is my Husband's scent." Is it because of that? Or is it because I said, "The myna of our house knows all that has happened"? Is it for this reason, or some other? I do not know. Is it for this reason, or some other? I do not know. The flower-like face of my lady-in-waiting broke into a sweat, and the one who lovingly raised me also looked scorched with dismay. Those who string garlands of words do so tirelessly. I do not know the full extent of the thoughts of the approaching King of Dance, Natarajar.
commentary: Her whole body now smells of camphor, and she says it is her Husband's scent: the sign that God has truly united with her. She calls the house myna as her witness. Her confidante (pāṅki) breaks into a sweat, her foster-mother's face looks scorched, and the gossips keep stringing their 'garlands of words.' She is caught between an undeniable inner reality and a world that sees only scandal.

translit: maṉṉutiruc capainaṭuvē maṇavāḷa ruṭaṉē vaḻakkāṭi valatupeṟṟēṉ eṉṟaata ṉālō iṉṉumavar vataṉa:iḷa nakaikāṇac celvēṉ eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ miṉṉumiṭaip pāṅkioru vitamāka naṭantāḷ mikapparivāl vaḷarttavaḷum veytuyirttup pōṉāḷ aṉṉanaṭaip peṇkaḷelām ciṉṉamoḻi pukaṉṟār attarnaṭa rāyartiruc cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, 'In the middle of the eternal, sacred hall, I argued my case with my Bridegroom and won'? Or is it because I said, 'I will go again to see the gentle smile on his face'? Is it for this reason, or some other? I do not know. My lady-in-waiting with the lightning-flash waist began to act strangely. The one who raised me with great affection sighed heavily and left. All the women with swan-like gaits spoke slighting words. I do not know the holy will of Father Natarajar, the King of Dance.
commentary: Claiming a personal, intimate relationship with God can sound like arrogance to those who view God as distant and unapproachable. The devotee speaks of her connection with a bride's familiarity, even saying she "won an argument" with her divine husband. This boldness shocks her companions, who only see transgressive behavior, not the deep intimacy it represents.

translit: kaḷḷuṇṭāḷ eṉappukaṉṟīr kaṉakacapai naṭuvē kaṇṭatalāl uṇṭatilai eṉṟaata ṉālō eḷḷuṇṭa maṟṟavarpōl eṉṉainiṉai yātīr eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ uḷḷuṇṭa makiḻccielām uvaṭṭiniṉṟāḷ pāṅki uvantuvaḷart tavaḷumeṉpāl civantakaṇṇaḷ āṉāḷ tuḷḷuṇṭa peṇkaḷelām cūḻntunoṭik kiṉṟār cuttarnaṭa rāyartiruc cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: You all claimed that I drank liquor. Is it because I replied, 'In the middle of the Golden Hall, I saw, but I did not consume'? Or is it because I said, 'Do not think of me like other, scorned women'? Is it for this reason, or some other? I do not know. All the inner joy of my lady-in-waiting turned to disgust. The one who lovingly raised me became red-eyed with anger towards me. The frivolous women all gather around, mocking me by snapping their fingers. I do not know the holy will of the Pure One, Natarajar, the King of Dance.
commentary: The ecstasy of divine union can look like simple drunkenness to an outside observer. People accuse the devotee of being intoxicated, and she must defend herself by explaining that her bliss comes from a vision of God in the Golden Hall (Kaṉakasapai at Chidambaram), not from liquor. Her plea not to be treated like a scorned woman reveals the pain of being judged by a world that cannot understand her spiritual state.

translit: kārikaiyīr ellīrum kāṇavammiṉ eṉatu kaṇavaraḻa kiṉaieṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi ērikavāt tiruvuruvai eḻutamuṭi yātē eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ kārikavāk kuḻalcōrak kaṭutteḻuntāḷ pāṅki kaṇpoṟuttu vaḷarttavaḷum puṇpoṟuttāḷ uḷattē nērikavāp peṇkaḷmoḻip pōrikavā teṭuttār niruttarnaṭa rāyartiruk karuttaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, 'O ladies, all of you, come and see my husband's beauty'? Or is it because I said, 'It is impossible to draw his sacred form of unsurpassable beauty'? Is it for this reason, or some other? I do not know. My lady-in-waiting rose up in anger, her beautiful hair coming loose. The one who raised me, watching over me, now bears a wound in her heart. The women with incomparable hair have launched an inescapable war of words. I do not know the holy intention of the Dancer, Natarajar, the King of Dance.
commentary: Trying to describe the indescribable beauty of God to those who cannot see it often leads to conflict instead of understanding. The devotee lovingly invites the other women to witness her divine husband's beauty, but they respond with anger. Her words, born of love, only start a "war of words," leaving her to conclude that the divine form cannot be captured or conveyed to an unwilling audience.

translit: kaṇṇēṟu paṭumeṉanāṉ añcukiṉṟēṉ eṉatu kaṇavarvaṭi vatukāṇaṟ keṉṟaata ṉālō eṇṇāta maṉattavarkaḷ kāṇaviḻai kiṉṟār eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ naṇṇāril kaṭuttamukam tōḻipeṟṟāḷ avaḷai nalkieṉai vaḷarttavaḷum malkiyavaṉ paṭuttāḷ peṇṇāyam palapalavum pēcukiṉṟār iṅkē periyanaṭa rāyaruḷḷap piriyamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, 'I am afraid my husband's form will attract the evil eye if people look upon it'? Or is it because I said, 'Those with unthinking minds desire to see him'? Is it for this reason, or some other? I do not know. My companion's face grew as furious as an enemy's. The one who gave me my companion and raised me now inflicts overwhelming cruelty upon me. Here, the circles of women are saying many, many things. I do not know the inner desire of the great King of Dance, Natarajar.
commentary: The devotee's love for God is so tender and protective that she fears even the "evil eye" (kaṇṇēṟu, a glance thought to cause harm) might mar his beauty. This deeply personal concern is the final straw for her community. Her closest companions turn on her with cruelty, and the circles of women gossip. She is left utterly alone, still questioning the ultimate intention behind her beloved's actions.

translit: kaṟpūram koṇarntuvammiṉ eṉkaṇavar vantāl kaṇṇeccil kaḻikkaeṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi eṟpūta nilaiyavartam tiruvaṭittā maraikkīḻ eṉṟucoṉṉēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ vaṟpūta vaṉampōṉṟāḷ pāṅkiyavaḷ taṉaimuṉ makiḻntupeṟṟiṅ keṉaivaḷarttāḷ viṉaivaḷarttāḷ āṉāḷ viṟpūoḷ nutalmaṭavār coṟpōrcey kiṉṟār viṇṇilavu naṭarāyar eṇṇamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, “Bring camphor to ward off the evil eye when my husband comes”? Or is it because I spoke of being under the lotus feet of him whose state transcends the elements? I do not know why. My friend has become like a jungle of mighty demons. The one who joyfully raised me has become one who cultivates my suffering. The women with bright, bow-like foreheads are waging a war of words. I do not know the intention of my Lord Natarajar, who dances in the celestial expanse.
commentary: The soul's devotion takes the form of simple, everyday ritual: preparing camphor to ward off the evil eye. Yet this is met with a "demonic" rage from her friend. The contrast between the simple act of love and the world's violent reaction shows how badly a mystical state can be misinterpreted by others as a kind of madness or spiritual transgression.

translit: maṉaiaṇainta malaraṇaimēl eṉaiaṇainta pōtu vaṭivucuka vaṭivāṉēṉ eṉṟaata ṉālō iṉaivaṟiyēṉ muṉpurinta peruntavameṉ pukalvēṉ eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ puṉaimukamōr karimukamāyp poṅkiniṉṟāḷ pāṅki puḻuṅkumaṉat tavaḷāki aḻuṅkukiṉṟāḷ cevili paṉaiyularnta ōlaieṉap peṇkaḷolik kiṉṟār paṇṇavareṉ naṭarāyar eṇṇamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, “When he embraced me on the flower bed in our home, I became a very form of bliss”? Or is it because I declared, “What great penance I must have done before! I am at a loss to describe it”? I do not know why. My friend’s decorated face has swelled with rage, turning dark. My foster-mother is deeply distressed, her mind sweltering. The other women make a racket like rustling dry palm leaves. I do not know the intention of my Lord Natarajar, praised by the celestials.
commentary: Here, the soul describes the pinnacle of spiritual union: she became bliss itself. But her attempt to share this ultimate experience only brings pain. Her friend's face darkens with rage, and her foster-mother (cevili) is tormented. This gap in understanding shows that the highest states of consciousness cannot be communicated; they can only be experienced, leaving the mystic isolated from those who have not shared the journey.

translit: tāḻkuḻalīr eṉaiccaṟṟē taṉikkaviṭṭāl eṉatu talaivaraikkāṇ kuvaleṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi ēḻkaṭaliṟ peritaṉṟō nāṉpeṟṟa iṉpam eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ kūḻkotippa teṉakkotittāḷ pāṅkieṉai vaḷartta kōtaimaruṇ ṭāṭukiṉṟa pētaieṉal āṉāḷ cūḻmaṭantai mārkaḷelām tūṟṟinakaik kiṉṟār cuttarnaṭa rāyartiruc cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, “O women with flowing hair, if you just leave me alone for a bit, I will see my Lord”? Or is it because I declared, “The bliss I received is greater than the seven seas”? I do not know why. My friend boiled with rage like bubbling porridge. The lady who raised me acts like a girl possessed, completely bewildered. All the women around me are slandering and laughing at me. I do not know the sacred will of the pure Lord Natarajar.
commentary: The soul's need for solitude to connect with God is seen by others as selfishness. Her declaration of immeasurable bliss is heard as a boast. The world responds with mockery and ridicule, pathologizing her state as a kind of possession or madness. The verse captures the painful dilemma of the mystic: the very conditions needed for spiritual life create friction with the social world.

translit: taṉittalaivar varukiṉṟa taruṇamitu maṭavīr taṉikkaeṉai viṭumiṉeṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi iṉittacuvai ellāmeṉ kaṇavaraṭic cuvaiyē eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ paṉittakuḷir kālattē caṉittacalam pōṉṟāḷ pāṅkieṉai vaḷarttavaḷum tūṅkumukaṅ koṇṭāḷ kaṉittapaḻam viṭuttumiṉṉār kāytiṉṉu kiṉṟār karuttarnaṭa rāyartiruk karuttaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, “O foolish women, this is the moment my peerless Lord is arriving, leave me alone!”? Or is it because I declared, “All sweet tastes are merely the taste of my husband’s feet”? I do not know why. My friend became like icy water born in the cold season. The one who raised me wears a dejected, drooping face. The lightning-like women have rejected ripe fruit and are eating unripe ones instead. I do not know the sacred intention of the primal Lord Natarajar.
commentary: The companions' anger turns to cold dejection. The last image echoes the Tirukkuṟaḷ (100): to speak harsh words when sweet ones are at hand is like leaving ripe fruit to eat unripe. Offered the sweetness she speaks of, the taste of her Husband's feet, the women answer with bitter words, and she is left alone with God, misunderstood by all.

translit: arumpoṉaṉai yāreṉatu turaivarumōr camayam akalaniṉmiṉ aṇaṅkaṉaiyīr eṉṟaata ṉālō irumpumaṇam āṉālum iḷakiviṭuṅ kaṇṭāl eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ karumpaṉaiyāḷ pāṅkiyumnāyk kaṭukaṉaiyāḷ āṉāḷ kaḷitteṉṉai vaḷarttavaḷum puḷittiṉṟāḷ ottāḷ virumpukiṉṟa peṇkaḷelām arumpukiṉṟār alartāṉ vittakareṉ naṭarāyar cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, “O you who are like rare gold, you who are like goddesses, my master is about to arrive, please stand aside”? Is it because I said, "O you who are like goddesses, stand aside: this is the moment my Master, who is like rare gold, is arriving"? Or is it because I said, "Even a heart of iron would melt at the sight of Him"? I do not know why. I do not know why. My friend, who was like sugarcane, has become like bitter dog’s mustard. The one who joyfully raised me now looks as if she has eaten tamarind. The curious women around me are all budding with scandal. I do not know the mind of the great adept, my Lord Natarajar.
commentary: The changing power of grace is obvious to the one who has experienced it, but it remains a mystery to those who have not. The speaker insists that the Lord's presence can soften even the hardest heart, but her friends' reactions show they remain untouched. Their sweetness turns to bitterness, a powerful metaphor for how the world sours in the face of a spiritual experience it does not share.

translit: maṇavāḷar varukiṉṟa taruṇamitu maṭavīr maṟaintirumiṉ nīvireṉṟēṉ ataṉālō aṉṟi eṇamētu numakkeṉaittāṉ yārtaṭukkak kūṭum eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ kuṇanīṭu pāṅkiavaḷ emmiṟaiyai niṉaiyār kuṇaṅkoṇṭāḷ vaḷarttavaḷum paṇamviṇṭāḷ āṉāḷ maṇanīṭu kuḻaṉmaṭavār kuṇanīṭu kiṉṟār vaḷḷalnaṭa rāyartiru vuḷḷamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, "Young women, this is the moment the Bridegroom is arriving, you must hide"? Or is it because I said, "What do you think you are doing? Who could possibly stop me?" I do not know for what reason. My virtuous lady-friend has taken on the character of those who do not think of my Lord. My foster-mother now speaks venomously. The young women with long, fragrant hair are behaving ever more strangely. I do not know the holy will of the generous King of Dance, Natarāyar.
commentary: As spiritual conviction deepens, the soul may act in ways that the world perceives as arrogant or antisocial. The speaker's urgent need for a private encounter with God, the Bridegroom, clashes with social norms. Her declaration that nothing can stop her is a statement of spiritual fact for her, but it sounds like a defiant challenge to her friends, who react with hostility.

translit: pativarumōr taruṇamitu nīviravar vaṭivaip pārppataṟkut taramillīr eṉṟaata ṉālō etilumeṉak kiccaiillai avaraṭikkaṇ allāl eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ matimukattāḷ pāṅkioru vitimukattāḷ āṉāḷ makiḻnteṉṉai vaḷarttavaḷum ikaḻntupala pukaṉṟāḷ tuticeymaṭa mātarelām caticeyvār āṉār cuttarnaṭa rāyartiruc cittamaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, "This is the moment the Lord is coming; you are not worthy to look upon His form"? Or is it because I said, "I have no desire for anything except for His holy feet"? I do not know for what reason. My lady-friend with the moon-like face has become one with the face of destiny. The one who raised me with joy now scorns me and says many insulting things. All the naive women who praised me have become conspirators. I do not know the holy mind of the Pure King of Dance, Natarāyar.
commentary: This verse portrays the painful climax of the soul's separation from the world. The speaker's blunt statement that others are not worthy to see God, combined with her total indifference to worldly things, causes the final break. Former admirers become enemies, and praise turns to conspiracy, leaving her utterly alone and bewildered, abandoned by the world yet still awaiting God's final grace.

translit: maṉṟāṭuṅ kaṇavartiru vārttaiaṉṟi umatu vārttaieṉṟaṉ cevikkēṟā teṉṟaata ṉālō iṉṟāvi aṉṉavarkkut taṉitta:iṭaṅ kāṇēṉ eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ muṉṟāṉai aviḻntuviḻa muṭukinaṭak kiṉṟāḷ mutaṟpāṅki vaḷarttavaḷum matarppuṭaṉcel kiṉṟāḷ oṉṟāta maṉappeṇkaḷ veṉṟāriṉ aṭuttār oruttanaṭa rāyartiruk karuttaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, "Except for the sacred words of my Husband who dances in the hall, your words will not enter my ears"? Or is it because I said, "Today I cannot find a private place for Him, who is my very life"? I do not know for what reason. My primary lady-friend rushes about, the front of her sari falling loose. My foster-mother walks away with arrogance. The women with disharmonious minds approach me as if they have won. I do not know the holy intention of the unique King of Dance, Natarāyar.
commentary: The soul's total dedication to God, to the point of rejecting all worldly advice, is seen by others as a kind of madness. Her family and friends react with confusion and contempt, unable to understand her inner state. Her final plea shows her complete bewilderment; she cannot grasp the divine intention behind her deep sense of abandonment.

translit: kūṭiyaeṉ kaṇavareṉaik kūṭāmaṟ kalaikkak kūṭuvatō nummālē eṉṟaata ṉālō ēṭieṉai aṟiyārō capaikkuvaru vārō eṉṟuraittēṉ itaṉālō etaṉālō aṟiyēṉ nāṭiyaeṉ pāṅkimaṉa mūṭiniṉṟu pōṉāḷ naṇṇieṉai vaḷarttavaḷum eṇṇiyavā ṟicaittāḷ tēṭiyaā yaṅkaḷelām kūṭiuraik kiṉṟār tiruttarnaṭa rāyartiruk karuttaiaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: Is it because I said, "Is it possible for you to disrupt my union with my Husband, who is already united with me?" Or is it because I said, "Hey girl, does He not know me? Will He come to the assembly hall?" I do not know for what reason. My dear lady-friend stood with a closed mind and left. The one who raised me closely spoke whatever came to her mind. All the companies of friends I sought have gathered and are talking amongst themselves. I do not know the holy intention of the perfect King of Dance, Natarāyar.
commentary: The soul's conviction in her inner union with God is unshakable, yet she is baffled by the hostility of the outside world. Her friends, unable to comprehend her experience, simply withdraw or gossip among themselves. This poem uses the traditional image of a young woman passionately in love to portray the soul's often lonely and misunderstood way toward the divine.

sections.title: The Mother's Report to the Foster Mother

translit: uṇarntavar tamakkum uṇarvari yāṉeṉ uḷḷakat tamarntaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ aṇintaṉaṉ eṉakkē aruṇmaṇa mālai aticayam aticayam eṉṟāḷ tuṇintunāṉ taṉitta pōtuvan teṉkai toṭṭaṉaṉ piṭittaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ puṇarntaṉaṉ kalantāṉ eṉṟuḷē kaḷittup poṅkiṉāḷ nāṉpeṟṟa poṉṉē.
translation: "He who is difficult to know even for those who know has settled within my heart," she said. "He adorned me with the wedding garland of grace, a wonder, a wonder!" she said. "When I was alone and resolute, he came, touched my hand, and held it," she said. "He united with me, he mingled with me!", saying this, the golden one I bore overflowed with inner bliss.
commentary: In a complete shift from the previous poem's anguish, the soul now experiences blissful union. The birth mother relays her daughter's words of wonder: God, once thought to be impossibly distant, has come to reside within her heart. The spiritual path is portrayed as a sacred marriage, with God himself bestowing the "wedding garland of grace" and mingling with the soul in an intimate embrace.

translit: taṉipperum patiyē eṉpati ākat tavametu purintatō eṉṟāḷ aṉittanīt teṉaittāṉ aṉpiṉāl aṇaittāṉ aticayam aticayam eṉṟāḷ iṉittuyar ciṟitum aṭaintiṭēṉ eṉṟāḷ eṉakkiṇai yārkolō eṉṟāḷ caṉippiṟap paṟuttēṉ eṉṟuḷē kaḷipput tatumpiṉāḷ nāṉpeṟṟa taṉiyē.
translation: "What penance did I perform for the sole great Lord to become my husband?" she asked. "He removed all that is impermanent and embraced me with love, a wonder, a wonder!" she said. "Henceforth, I will not suffer in the least," she declared. "Who is my equal now?" she asked. The peerless one I bore brimmed with inner joy, saying, "I have severed the cycle of birth!"
commentary: The daughter's joy overflows as she reflects on this divine union. She has been embraced by the "sole great Lord," an act that has freed her from all worldly suffering and severed the cycle of birth and death. Her ecstatic question, "Who is my equal now?" is an expression of the supreme freedom and fulfillment that comes from realizing God.

translit: puṇṇiya patiyaip puṇarntaṉaṉ nāṉcey puṇṇiyam pukalari teṉṟāḷ taṇṇiya matiyiṉ amuteṉak kaḷitta tayavaināṉ maṟappaṉō eṉṟāḷ eṇṇiya aṉaittum īntaruḷ kiṉṟāṉ eṉṉaiyō eṉṉaiyō eṉṟāḷ aṇṇiya pērā ṉantamē vaṭivam āyiṉāḷ nāṉpeṟṟa aṇaṅkē.
translation: "I have united with the Lord of all merit; the merit I performed to achieve this is beyond words," she said. "How could I ever forget the kindness he bestowed, like nectar from the cool moon?" she asked. "He graciously grants everything I think of, oh my, oh my!" she cried. The divine girl I bore became the very form of immense, approaching bliss.
commentary: Having united with God, the soul's own nature begins to change. Its thoughts are now instantly fulfilled because its will is aligned with the divine will. The experience of grace is so full that the soul becomes the very embodiment of bliss. The girl's transformation shows that union with God is an event and a change in the very substance of one's being.

translit: cattiya ñāṉa capāpati eṉakkē taṉippati āyiṉāṉ eṉṟāḷ nittiya vāḻvu peṟṟunāṉ iṉpa nilaitaṉil niṟaintaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ pittiyal ulakīr kāṇmiṉō cittip pēṟelām eṉvacat teṉṟāḷ etticai yīrum ottivaṇ varuka eṉṟaṉaḷ eṉatumel liyalē.
translation: "Sathiya Gnana Sabapathi has become my one and only lord," she said. "Having gained eternal life, I am now filled with a state of bliss," she said. "O people of this mad world, look! All the attainments of siddhi are now in my possession," she declared. "People from every direction, come here together in accord!" called out my delicate one.
commentary: The soul, having attained eternal life and supernatural powers (siddhi), does not keep this prize to itself. It calls out to the "mad world," inviting everyone to witness this new reality. This reveals a core principle of Vallalar's path: enlightenment is a state to be shared with all humanity. Sathiya Gnana Sabapathi (Lord of the Hall of True Wisdom) is Vallalar's name for the supreme reality revealed in this state.

translit: tirumaṇip potuvil oruperum patieṉ cintaiyil kalantaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ perumaiyil ciṟantēṉ eṉperun tavattaip pēcutal aritari teṉṟāḷ irumaiyum eṉpōl orumaiyil peṟṟār yāṇṭuḷar yāṇṭuḷar eṉṟāḷ marumalar mukattē iḷanakai tuḷumpa vayaṅkiṉāḷ nāṉpeṟṟa makaḷē.
translation: "The one great Lord of the sacred, jeweled common space has mingled with my mind," she said. "I have excelled in greatness; my great penance is too difficult to describe," she said. "Where, oh where, are there others who, like me, have gained both worlds in a state of oneness?" she asked. My own daughter shone brightly, a gentle smile overflowing on her fragrant, flower-like face.
commentary: The soul's union with God collapses the distinction between the spiritual and material worlds. By "gaining both worlds in a state of oneness," the soul is not waiting for a heavenly reward after death; it experiences the fullness of both realms simultaneously, right here and now. The "sacred, jeweled common space" is the boundless, universal consciousness where this union takes place.

translit: vaḷḷalaip puṇarntēṉ ammavō itutāṉ mālaiyō kālaiyō eṉṟāḷ eḷḷalait tavirntēṉ ulakelām eṉakkē ēvalcey kiṉṟaṉa eṉṟāḷ teḷḷamu tarunti aḻivilā uṭampum cittiyum peṟṟaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ tuḷḷiya maṭavīr kāṇmiṉō eṉṟāḷ cōrvilāḷ nāṉpeṟṟa cutaiyē.
translation: "I have united with the generous Lord! Oh, is this evening or morning?" she said. "I am free from all scorn; all the worlds now do my bidding," she said. "I have drunk the clear nectar, gaining an indestructible body and siddhi," she said. "O joyful young women, come see!" she said. She is the tireless one, the daughter I bore.
commentary: The transformation is so complete that the soul loses its sense of ordinary time, asking if it is morning or evening. It has drunk the nectar of grace and attained an "indestructible body," a central and unique teaching of Vallalar. It is a literal, physical transformation into a deathless being, a state of perfect freedom where even the cosmos obeys one's will.

translit: kaṉakamā maṉṟil naṭampuri pataṅkaḷ kaṇṭaṉaṉ kaṇṭaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ aṉakaciṟ capaiyil oruperum patieṉ aṉpilē kalantaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ tiṉakara cōmāk kiṉielām eṉakkē ceyalceyat tantaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ taṉakarat teṉaittāṉ taḻuviṉāṉ eṉṟāḷ tavattiṉāl peṟṟanam taṉiyē.
translation: "I have seen, I have seen the feet that dance in the great golden hall!" she said. "In the flawless hall of consciousness, the one great Lord has mingled with my love," she said. "He has granted that the sun, moon, and fire all act for me," she said. "He embraced me with his own hands," she said. She is the unique one we gained through penance.
commentary: The "great golden hall" is a metaphor for the heart or the center of consciousness, where God is perceived as dancing. The soul's union is an intimate, personal embrace founded on love. As a direct result of this loving relationship, even cosmic forces like the sun, moon, and fire now act according to the soul's will.

translit: koṭipperu maṇippoṟ kōyileṉ uḷamāk koṇṭuvan tamarntaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ kaṭipputu malarppūṅ kaṇṇivēyn teṉaittāṉ kaṭimaṇam purintaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ oṭippaṟa ellām vallatōr cittām oḷieṉak kaḷittaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ iṭippoṭu noṭittīr kāṇmiṉō eṉṟāḷ eṉtavat tiyaṉṟamel liyalē.
translation: "He took my heart as his great, flag-adorned, jeweled, golden temple and came to abide there," she said. "He crowned me with a fragrant garland of fresh flowers and performed the sacred marriage with me," she said. "He bestowed on me the Light, the Siddhi that can do all things without fail," she said. "You who scorned me with thunderous words, look now!" she said. She is the tender one created by my penance.
commentary: The union is now described using the powerful metaphor of a sacred marriage, with God making the soul's heart his own temple. This divine marriage bestows an ultimate power, a form of siddhi: a divine light of omnipotence. Her final cry is one of triumph, a vindication against all who had previously scorned her spiritual path.

translit: vāḻimā maṇimaṉ ṟiṟaivaṉē eṉakku mālaivan taṇintaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ ūḻitō ṟūḻi ulaviṉum aḻiyā uṭampeṉak kaḷittaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ āḻicūḻ ulakō ṭaṇṭaṅkaḷ aṉaittum aḷikkaeṉ ṟaruḷiṉāṉ eṉṟāḷ ēḻiyaṉ māṭa micaiyuṟa vaittāṉ eṉṟaṉaḷ eṉatumel liyalē.
translation: "The Lord of the glorious, great jeweled hall himself came and placed a garland on me," she said. "He gave me a body that will not perish, even if it roams for eon after eon," she said. "He graciously commanded me to protect all the worlds surrounded by the sea and all the universes," she said. "He placed me high upon a seven-storied mansion," said my tender one.
commentary: The divine union elevates the soul to a position of cosmic authority. She is granted an immortal body and the sacred duty to protect all of creation. The "seven-storied mansion" is a classic symbol for a high and unshakeable state of spiritual consciousness, signifying her permanent establishment in this new reality.

translit: ēlunaṉ maṇimā maṉṟaruṭ cōti eṉṉuḷat tamarntaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ pālumiṉ cuvaiyum pōṉṟeṉa tāvi paṟṟiṉaṉ kalantaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ cālumev vulakum taḻaikkaeṉ taṉakkē cattiyai aḷittaṉaṉ eṉṟāḷ mēlumek kālum aḻivilēṉ eṉṟāḷ mikukaḷip puṟṟaṉaḷ viyantē.
translation: "The Grace-Light from the fitting, great jeweled hall has settled in my heart," she said. "Like milk and its sweetness, he seized my soul and mingled with it," she said. "To me alone, he gave the sakti to make all worlds flourish as they should," she said. "I will never perish, now or ever," she said, filled with immense joy and wonder.
commentary: The poem concludes by defining the nature of this union as an inseparable mingling, like milk and its inherent sweetness. This union bestows sakti, the divine power, to sustain and nurture all worlds. The soul's final declaration is one of absolute certainty in her own immortality, a state of wondrous joy.

sections.title: The Greatness of the Sacred Feet

translit: tiruvāḷar kaṉakacapait tirunaṭañcey taruḷvār tēvarcikā maṇieṉakkut tirumālai koṭuttār uruvāḷar aruvāki oḷiyāki veḷiyāy ōṅkukiṉṟār eṉṉuṭaiya uyirttuṇaivar avartam peruvāymait tiṟamciṟitum pēcamuṭi yātē pēcuvatār maṟaikaḷelām kūcukiṉṟa eṉṟāl turuvāmal iṅkeṉakkuk kiṭaittataieṉ colvēṉ collaḷaval lātacukam tōṉṟuvateṉ tōḻi.
translation: The graceful One who graciously performs the sacred dance in the Golden Hall, the crest-jewel of the celestials, gave me a sacred garland. He has form, yet He becomes formless, light, and pure space, ever-transcending. He is my life-companion. It is impossible to speak even a little of the nature of His great truth. Who can speak of it, when even all the Vedas are abashed? What can I say about attaining this here, without even seeking it? A bliss that cannot be measured by words is dawning, O my friend.
commentary: The direct, personal experience of God's grace surpasses all scriptures and religious traditions. The devotee has been chosen by the divine dancer of the Golden Hall, a central image of God for Vallalar. She knows him as her intimate companion, yet she finds that his reality is beyond words, so vast that even the holy Vedas cannot describe it. The greatest miracle is that this immeasurable bliss came to her unsought.

translit: aruḷāḷar poṟpotuvil aṟputanā ṭakañcey āṉanta vaṇṇareṉai āḷuṭaiyār ciṟiyēṉ teruḷāta paruvattē teruṭṭimaṇam purinta cīrāḷar avarperumait tiṟattaievar pukalvār maruḷāta ākamaṅkaḷ māmaṟaikaḷ ellām maruṇṭaṉavē eṉṉaṭieṉ maṉavākkiṉ aḷavō iruḷāmai eṉṟuṟumō aṉṟuciṟi turaippēṉ eṉṉavumnāṇ īrppatitaṟ keṉpurivēṉ tōḻi.
translation: The gracious One, the One of blissful nature who performs a wondrous drama in the golden common space, is the One who rules me, a simple person. He is the glorious One who enlightened and married me in my unenlightened age. Who can declare the nature of His greatness? The unerring Agamas and all the great Vedas are themselves bewildered. So what, my friend, is the measure of my mind and speech? When the day comes that I am free from darkness, I will speak a little then. But even as I resolve to do so, shyness pulls me back. What can I do about this, O friend?
commentary: Divine grace is a gift freely given to the unenlightened. The devotee sees herself as simple and unknowing, yet God himself became her teacher and united with her. Faced with this immense grace, she feels that even the most sacred texts (Agamas and Vedas) are bewildered. Her own words feel entirely inadequate, and a sense of humble shyness prevents her from even trying to describe the experience.

translit: cempavaḷat tirumalaiyō māṇikka viḷakkō ceḻuñcōtit taṉippiḻampō cevvaṇṇat tiraḷō ampatumat tiruviḷaṅkum akalattāṉ piramaṉ araṉmutalōr aivarkaḷum appālniṉ ṟōrum emparameṉ ṟemperumāṉ puṟavaṇṇam etuvō eṉpārēl akavaṇṇam yāruraikka vallār tamparameṉ ṟeṉṉaiaṉṟu maṇampurintār kaṉaka capainātar avarperumai cāṟṟuvateṉ tōḻi.
translation: Is He a sacred mountain of red coral or a ruby lamp? A singular column of rich light or a mass of crimson color? If even the five great gods, Vishnu, who bears the lotus Goddess on his chest, Brahma, Siva, and their peers, and those beyond them all ask, “What is the outer form of our Supreme Lord?”, who then could possibly describe His inner form? He claimed me as his own and married me that day, the Lord of the Golden Hall, what can I say of his greatness, O friend?
commentary: God's true nature is utterly beyond human and even celestial comprehension. The devotee tries to capture God's form with radiant images, but then realizes the futility of it. If even the greatest gods of the cosmos do not know God's outer appearance, she asks, who could possibly know his inner reality? The mystery deepens the wonder that this same unknowable being chose to unite with her personally.

translit: tēvarkaḷō cittarkaḷō cīvaṉmuttar tāmō ciṟantamuṉit talaivarkaḷō cemporuḷkaṇ ṭōrō mūvarkaḷō aṟuvarkaḷō mutaṟcatti avaḷō muṉṉiyanam peruṅkaṇavar tamiyalai uṇarntōr yāvarkaḷum allaeṉṟāl yāṉuṇarntu colla amaiyumō oruciṟitum amaiyātu kaṇṭāy āvaloṭum aṉpartoḻak kaṉakacapai naṭippār avarperumai evvitattum avaraṟivār tōḻi.
translation: The devas? The siddhas? The jivanmuktas themselves? The greatest of sages? Those who have seen the ultimate reality? The Trimurti? The Six? The primordial Shakti herself? Who among these has understood the nature of our great husband whom we revere? If the answer is none of them, is it then fitting for me to understand and speak of it? It is not fitting in the slightest, you see. He dances in the Golden Hall as devotees worship Him with longing, in every way, He alone knows His own greatness, O friend.
commentary: The true reality of God is known only to God. The devotee lists the highest beings imaginable: devas (celestial beings), siddhas (perfected masters), jivanmuktas (souls liberated while in a body), sages, and even the primordial Shakti (divine feminine power). If none of these can grasp God's nature, she concludes, then it is impossible for her to do so. The poem ends with an attitude of deep humility before a mystery that only God himself comprehends.

translit: patiuṭaiyār kaṉakacapā patieṉumpēr uṭaiyār paṇamparittavaraiyareṉṉai maṇampurinta kaṇavar vitiyuṭaiyār ēttaniṉṟa tutiuṭaiyār ñāṉa viḷakkaṉaiya meyuṭaiyār veyyaviṉai aṟutta matiuṭaiyār tamakkaruḷum vaṇkaiperi tuṭaiyār maṅkaiciva kāmavalli maṇavāḷar muṭimēl natiuṭaiyār avarperumai maṟaikkumeṭṭā teṉṟāl nāṉuraikka māṭṭuvaṉō navilāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: He is the Lord of all; He bears the name Kanakasabhapathi. He is the King of the mountain of hooded serpents, the husband who married me. He is the object of praise, extolled by those who follow the sacred law. He has a body like a lamp of wisdom. He possesses a greatly generous hand, gracing the wise ones who have severed their harsh karma. He is the bridegroom of the maiden Sivakama Valli. He wears a river on His crown. If His greatness is beyond the reach of the Vedas, am I able to speak of it? Tell me, my friend.
commentary: God's reality is so vast that it transcends even the most sacred scriptures, the Vedas. The verse lists traditional titles for Siva, such as Kanakasabhapathi (Lord of the Golden Hall), but its central message is one of humility. If the holy books themselves cannot capture God's full greatness, the speaker asks, how could a mere individual hope to do so? This emphasizes that personal experience of the divine goes beyond what any text can contain.

translit: veṭittaḷinta mukkaṉiyiṉ vaṭittaracan taṉilē virumpuṟaniṉ ṟōṅkiyaceṅ karumpiratam kalantu taṭittaceḻum pāṟpeytu kōṟṟēṉviṭ ṭataṉait taṉittaparā amutattil tāṉkalantuṇ ṭāṟpōl iṭittiṭitteṉ uḷamuḻutum tittikkum vārttai iṉituraittu maṇampurinta eṉṉuyirnā yakarvāṉ poṭittirumē ṉiyarnaṭaṉam purikiṉṟār avartam pukaḻuraikka vallēṉō allēṉkāṇ tōḻi.
translation: Like consuming a blend of the filtered essence from the three choice fruits burst open and softened, the juice of tall red sugarcane, rich thick milk, and pure honey, all mixed into the unique, supreme nectar itself, so are the words he spoke. They strike my mind again and again, sweetening my entire being. My life’s Lord, who sweetly spoke and married me, his celestial body dusted with holy ash, is performing the dance. Am I capable of declaring his glory? I am not, you see, my friend.
commentary: The experience of divine communication is an overwhelming sweetness that defies description. Vallalar creates a vivid image of a supreme nectar made from the richest fruits, sugarcane, milk, and honey to convey the feeling of God's words entering the soul. This experience is a blissful taste that sweetens one's entire being, leaving the speaker unable to do anything but marvel.

translit: tirucciṟṟam palattiṉpat tiruurukkoṇ ṭaruḷām tirunaṭañcey taruḷukiṉṟa tiruvaṭikaḷ iraṇṭum aruccikkum pēraṉpar aṟiviṉkaṇ aṟivāy avvaṟivil viḷaintacivā ṉantaamu tāki uruccikkum paranātat talaṅkaṭantap pāṟcit turuvukaṭan tirukkumeṉa uṇarntōrcol vārēl peruccittel lāmvalla naṭarājap perumāṉ perumaiyaiyām pēcuvateṉ pēcāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: His two sacred feet have taken a blissful, sacred form in the holy Chit Sabhai and perform the dance of grace. They become the awareness within the awareness of the great devotees who worship them, and the nectar of divine bliss that arises in that awareness. If even the realized ones say that these feet exist beyond the form of consciousness itself, having crossed the intensely sought-after plane of supreme sound, then what can we say of the greatness of the great Lord Nataraja, who is master of all great powers? Tell me, my friend.
commentary: The divine grace, symbolized by God's dancing feet in the Chit Sabhai (hall of consciousness), is the ultimate source of a devotee's inner awareness and bliss. Yet, Vallalar explains that this source is more than within consciousness; it is beyond it. Even realized sages say that God's reality transcends the highest mystical planes, such as the supreme sound (paranāda). If the divine exists beyond consciousness itself, its true greatness is impossible for the conscious mind to grasp or express.

translit: nātavarai ceṉṟumaṟai ōraṉantam kōṭi nāṭiiḷait tiruntaṉaā kamaṅkaḷ paranāta pōtavarai pōntupala mukaṅkoṇṭu tēṭip puṇarppaṟiyā tiruntaṉaeṉ ṟaṟiñarpukal vārēl pātavarai veṇṟu paṭintilaṅkac cōtip paṭivameṭut tampalattē paratanaṭam puriyum pōtavaraik kāṇpatalāl avarperumai eṉṉāl pukalavaca māmōnī pukalāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: If the wise declare that countless billions of Vedas searched to the very boundary of sound and grew weary, and that the Agamas reached the shore of the awareness of supreme sound, took many forms to search, and still failed to unite with him, then how could it be in my power to declare the greatness of that Lord of consciousness, who conquered death, took a form of radiant light, and performs the supreme dance in the sacred hall? Beyond merely seeing him, is it possible? You tell me, my friend.
commentary: Even the most sacred scriptures, the Vedas and Agamas, are shown to be incapable of reaching or understanding God. Vallalar portrays them as seekers who searched to the very limits of reality and failed, growing weary in their quest. This powerfully elevates direct, grace-given experience, seeing the Lord's dance in the sacred hall, above all scriptural and intellectual knowledge. The final truth, he suggests, can only be witnessed.

translit: paraiirunta veḷimuḻutum paraviappāl paraiyiṉ paramāki apparattil paramparamāy viḷaṅkit tiraikaṭanta tiruveḷiyil āṉantā tītat tirunaṭañcey yātuceyum tiruvaṭikaḷ eṉṟē puraikaṭantōr pukalkiṉṟār kēṭkiṉṟōm eṉṟāl puṇṇiyareṉ taṉittalaivar puṉitanaṭa rājar varaikaṭanta tiruttōḷmēl tirunīṟṟar avartam vāymaicola vallēṉō allēṉkāṇ tōḻi.
translation: The flawless ones declare that his sacred feet spread throughout the entire expanse where the supreme power exists and beyond; that they are supreme even to that supreme power; that they shine as the supreme of the supreme in that state; and that they perform, without performing, the dance of bliss-beyond-bliss in the sacred space that has crossed all veils. If this is what we hear them say, am I able to speak the truth of my singular Lord, the holy Nataraja, the virtuous one with holy ash on his mountain-like shoulders? I am not, you see, my friend.
commentary: This verse describes God's nature as being utterly transcendent, existing beyond even the highest cosmic principles like Parai, the universal creative power. The most enlightened beings say His dance is a paradox: an action that is not an action, performed in a sacred space that is beyond all conceptual "veils" or limitations. Faced with such accounts, the speaker again expresses her own powerlessness to describe the Lord’s true nature.

translit: ēyppanti vaṇṇareṉṟum paṭikavaṇṇar eṉṟum iṇaiyiloḷi uruvareṉṟum iyalaruvar eṉṟum vāyppantal iṭutalaṉṟi uṇmaicola vallār maṇṇiṭattum viṇṇiṭattum maṟṟiṭattum ilaiyē kāyppanta marameṉṟu kaṇṭucolva taṉṟik kāyttavaṇṇam pūttavaṇṇam kaṇṭukoḷa māṭṭāt tāyppanta uṇarvuṭaiyēṉ yāṉōciṟ capaiyil taṉimutalvar tiruvaṇṇam cāṟṟavallēṉ tōḻi.
translation: People erect canopies of words, saying he is the color of the evening sky or the color of crystal, that he is a form of unrivaled light or that he is naturally formless. But besides this verbal display, there is no one on earth, in the heavens, or anywhere else who can speak his truth. My awareness is like that of one who recognizes a tree bears fruit but cannot perceive the manner of its blooming or fruiting. With such a dependent bond of feeling, am I, of all people, able to declare the sacred nature of the singular First Being in the Chit Sabhai, O friend?
commentary: All human attempts to describe God with words, whether by assigning him a form, a color, or declaring him formless, are dismissed as mere verbal decoration. The speaker compares her own understanding to someone who sees fruit on a tree but has no knowledge of the hidden process of its growth. Her knowing is superficial and dependent. With such limited awareness, she concludes, she is completely unqualified to speak of God's true being.

translit: kalaikkaṭalaik kaṭantamuṉik kaṇaṅkaḷummum malamām karicakaṉṟa yōkikaḷum kaṇṭukoḷa māṭṭā talaikkaṭalil turumpāki alaikiṉṟār maṉṟuḷ āṭukiṉṟār eṉpatalāl avarvaṇṇam atuvum nilaikkuriya tiruccapaiyiṉ vaṇṇamumac capaikkaṇ niruttattiṉ vaṇṇamumin nīrmaiyaṉa eṉṟē malaikkuniṟai kaṇṭālum kāṇavoṇā tamma vāyppatarkaḷ tūṟṟuvatil varumpayaṉeṉ tōḻi.
translation: Even throngs of sages who have crossed the ocean of scriptures, and yogis who are free from the stain of the three impurities, cannot perceive Him. They are tossed about like straw in the primordial ocean. Except for saying, “He dances in the hall,” they cannot define His nature, the nature of the eternal sacred hall, or the nature of the dance within that hall as being "of this specific quality." O friend, even if one could determine the weight of a mountain, this cannot be perceived. What use is there in worthless people blabbering?
commentary: Even the most accomplished spiritual masters, such as sages who have mastered every scripture and yogis who are free from the three core impurities (mum malam), are depicted as being utterly lost. They are tossed about helplessly, able only to state that the divine dance is happening, but completely unable to define its qualities or the nature of God. The verse concludes that trying to measure or define the divine is a futile and worthless effort.

translit: citamalarō cukamalarum parimaḷikka ōṅkum tirucciṟṟam palanaṭuvē tirunaṭaṉam puriyum patamalarō patamalaril pātukaiyō avaiyil paṭintatirup poṭiyōap poṭipaṭinta paṭiyō itamalarum appaṭimēl iruntavarō avarpēr icaittavarum kēṭṭavarum ilaṅkumuttar eṉṟāl nitamalarum naṭarājap perumāṉeṉ kaṇavar nilaiuraikka vallārār nikaḻttāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: In the middle of the holy Chitrambalam, where the flowers of consciousness and bliss spread their fragrance, He performs the sacred dance. His flower-feet; the sandals on those flower-feet; the sacred dust that settled on the sandals; the ground on which that dust settled; those who sat upon that ground where goodness blossoms: if even those who uttered their names and those who heard them shine as liberated ones, who is able to describe the state of my husband, the great Lord Nataraja, who blossoms ever new? Tell me, O friend.
commentary: Through a cascade of images Vallalar shows how far the power of the sacred feet reaches: from the feet to the sandals, to the dust on the sandals, to the ground where that dust fell, to those who sat on that ground. Even those who merely spoke or heard the names of such people shine as liberated souls. If grace overflows this far from the feet, who could ever describe the state of the Lord Himself?

translit: cuttamuṟṟa aimpūta veḷikaraṇa veḷimēl tulaṅkuveḷi turiyaveḷi cukaveḷiyē mutalām ittakaiya veḷikaḷuḷḷē evveḷiyō naṭaṉam iyaṟṟuveḷi eṉkiṉṟār eṉṟālav veḷiyil nittapari pūraṇamāy āṉanta mayamāy niruttamiṭum emperumāṉ nipuṇanaṭa rāyar citturuvām tiruvaṭiyiṉ uṇmaivaṇṇam aṟintu ceppuvatār eṉvacamō ceppāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: They ask, among all the expanses, beginning with the pure expanse of the five elements, the expanse of the inner instruments, the radiant expanse above that, the expanse of Turiya, and the expanse of bliss, which one is the expanse where He performs the dance? If this is so, who can know and speak the true nature of the sacred feet, the very form of consciousness, belonging to our Lord, the expert King of Dance, who dances in that expanse as eternally perfect and full of bliss? Is it within my power? Tell me, O friend.
commentary: The divine dance takes place in an expanse that transcends all known levels of reality. People speculate whether it is in the space of the five elements, the inner faculties (karanas), or even the high spiritual state of Turiya (the fourth state of consciousness). Vallalar says God's true dance floor contains all these but is not limited by any of them. His essence is pure consciousness, and no one can truly grasp the reality of His dance in that ultimate expanse.

translit: kāṟṟuruvō kaṉaluruvō kaṭavuḷuru eṉpār kāṟṟuruvum kaṉaluruvum kaṇṭuraippīr eṉṟāl vēṟṟuruvē pukalvaratai vēṟoṉṟāl maṟuttāl viḻittuviḻit tempōlvār mikavummaruḷ kiṉṟār tōṟṟumantat tattuvamum tōṟṟāttat tuvamum turicāka avaikaṭanta cukacorupam āki māṟṟamaṉam uṇarvucellāt talattāṭum perumāṉ vaṭivuraikka vallavarār vaḻuttāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: Some say God’s form is of air or of fire. If you ask them to describe the forms of air and fire they have seen, they will speak of some other form. If you refute that with something else, they stare wide-eyed, like us, and become utterly confused. He is the very form of bliss, having swiftly transcended both the manifest principles and the unmanifest principles. Who is able to describe the form of the great Lord who dances in a place where speech, mind, and consciousness cannot go? Praise Him, O friend.
commentary: People's attempts to define God's form, whether as air, fire, or anything else, quickly fall apart under questioning. God's reality is not a physical element nor is it one of the philosophical principles (tattvas) that make up the universe. He is the form of pure bliss, dancing in a place that mind, speech, and even consciousness cannot enter, making His true form impossible to describe.

translit: nātamaṭṭum ceṉṟaṉammēl cellavaḻi aṟiyēm naviṉṟapara vintumaṭṭum nāṭiṉammēl aṟiyēm ētamilāp paranāta ellaimaṭṭum ceṉṟēm iṉiccella vaḻikāṇēm ilaṅkuperuveḷikkē ātaravil ceṉṟaṉammēl cellavaḻi teriyēm ammamma eṉṟumaṟai ākamaṅkaḷ ellām ōtaniṉṟa tirunaṭaṉap perumāṉār vaṭiviṉ uṇmaicola vallavarār uraiyāreṉ tōḻi.
translation: The Vedas and Agamas all stand and proclaim in awe, “We went as far as Natham, but we do not know the way beyond. We sought as far as the proclaimed Para Vintu, but we do not know what is beyond. We went to the border of the flawless Paranatham, but now we see no way to proceed. We went with devotion to the radiant great expanse, but we do not know the way beyond.” Who, then, is able to speak the truth of the form of the great Lord of the sacred dance? Tell me, O friend.
commentary: The most sacred scriptures, the Vedas and Agamas (ancient collections of spiritual wisdom), themselves confess that they cannot reach the ultimate reality. They declare in awe that they reached the limits of mystical states like Natham (primordial sound) and Para Vintu (the transcendent point), but could not find the way beyond. If these highest sources of spiritual knowledge admit their own limitations, then no mortal could possibly describe the true form of the Lord of the Dance.

translit: tōṉṟucatti palakōṭi aḷavucola oṇṇāt tōṟṟucatti palakōṭit tokaiuraikka muṭiyā cāṉṟulakam tōṟṟuvikkum cattipala kōṭi taṉaiviḷampal ākāac cattikaḷaik kūṭṭi ēṉṟavakai viṭukkiṉṟa cattipala kōṭi ittaṉaikkum atikāri eṉkaṇavar eṉṟāl āṉṟamaṇi maṉṟiliṉpa vaṭivāki naṭikkum avarperumai evaruraippār aṟiyāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: There are countless crores of manifest Saktis, and countless crores of originating Saktis whose number cannot be told. There are countless crores of Saktis that create the evident worlds, which are impossible to describe. There are countless crores of Saktis that gather and dispatch those Saktis as needed. If my husband is the master of all these, who can describe the greatness of him who performs as the form of bliss in the perfect, gem-like Hall? You do not understand, my friend.
commentary: The creative power of God is infinite, operating on a scale too vast to imagine. Vallalar expresses this through the voice of a devotee speaking of her divine beloved. She describes countless types of Saktis (divine powers) that create and manage the cosmos. If her Lord is the master of this entire immensity, his true nature as the form of bliss dancing in the sacred Hall (Manram) is utterly beyond description.

translit: tōṟṟamoṉṟē vaṭivoṉṟu vaṇṇamoṉṟu viḷaṅkum cōtioṉṟu maṟṟataṉil tulaṅkumiyal oṉṟu āṟṟaatil paramāya aṇuoṉṟu pakuti atuoṉṟu pakutikkuḷ amaintakaru oṉṟu ēṟṟamikka akkaruvuḷ cattioṉṟu cattik kiṟaioṉṟām ittaṉaikkum eṉkaṇavar allāl āṟṟamaṟṟōr atikāri illaiyaṭi maṉṟil āṭumavar peruntakaimai yāruraippār tōḻi.
translation: There is a single origin, a single form, a single color, a single effulgence that shines, and a single nature that is radiant within it. Within that power is a single supreme atom, a single fundamental substance, and a single seed-conceptset within that substance. Within that excellent seed-concept is a single Sakti, and for that Sakti, a single Lord. For all of these, there is no other authority but my husband. Who can describe the greatness of him who dances in the Hall, my friend?
commentary: Creation unfolds from a single, unified source, yet it contains all of existence within it. Vallalar lists a chain of "ones": one origin, one form, one supreme atom (anu), one fundamental substance (pakuti), one seed-concept (karu), one power (Sakti), and one Lord over it all. The message is that the universe's immense complexity is held and governed by a single, supreme consciousness whose true greatness is unknowable.

translit: orumaipeṟu tōṟṟamoṉṟu tattuvampal vēṟu oṉṟiṉiyal oṉṟiṭattē uṟṟila:iṅ kivaṟṟai irumaiyiṉum mummaimutal eḻumaiyiṉum kūṭṭi ilaṅkiyaciṟ cattinaṭu iraṇṭoṉṟeṉ ṉāta perumaipeṟṟu viḷaṅkaatiṉ naṭuaruḷniṉ ṟilaṅkap periyaaruḷ naṭuniṉṟu turiyanaṭam puriyum arumaievar kaṇṭukoḷvar avarperumai avarē aṟiyārē eṉṉaṭinī aṟaintavaṇṇam tōḻi.
translation: The origin is one, but its principles are many and varied; the nature of one is not found in another. Here, combining them in pairs, triplets, and up to sets of seven, the radiant Chit-Sakti shines in the center with the greatness of being indivisibly one-and-two. In its center, Grace stands shining. In the center of that great Grace, he performs the Turiya dance. Who can perceive this rarity? He himself does not even know his own greatness. What is this you have said, my friend?
commentary: Though the universe appears as many different principles (tattvas), a single divine consciousness holds it all together. This power, Chit-Sakti (Sakti of consciousness), unifies everything. At the very center of this is Grace, and within Grace, the Lord performs the Turiya dance, a dance symbolizing a state of pure awareness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. This reality is so deep, Vallalar says, that even the Lord seems unaware of his own greatness, showing how completely it transcends our understanding.

translit: paṭaittapaṭaip poṉṟatilē paramatiṟkā raṇamām pakutiatil pakukkiṉṟa paṇikaḷpala palavām puṭaittaavai pukuntulavum puramoṉṟap purattil pūpatioṉ ṟavarkkuṇarttum pūraṇacit toṉṟu miṭaitta:ivai ellāñciṟ ṟampalattē naṭikkum meṉpatattōr ciṟṟiṭattu viḷaṅkinilai peṟavē aṭaittumaṟṟiṅ kivaikkellām appuṟattē niṟpār avarperumai evaraṟivār aṟiyāynī tōḻi.
translation: In the one creation he made is the supreme, causal substance. Within it, the functions that differentiate are many. There is a single city where these expand and roam. In that city is a single king, and there is a single, perfect consciousness that informs him. He confines all these crowded things to shine and be established within a tiny space of his soft foot that dances in the Chithambalam, and yet he stands beyond all of them. Who knows his greatness? You do not know, my friend.
commentary: The entire cosmos, with all its complexity, is contained within a tiny space on the Lord's foot as he dances. Vallalar uses this startling image to show God's simultaneous presence within creation and transcendence beyond it. Everything exists within the Chithambalam (hall of consciousness), yet He remains separate and untouched. His true nature, which both contains and exceeds everything, is completely beyond our grasp.

translit: ciruṭṭioṉṟu ciṟṟaṇuvil ciṟitataṉil ciṟitu ciṉaittakara ṇakkaruac ciṉaikkaruvil ciṟitu veruṭṭiyamāṉ ammāṉil ciṟitumati matiyiṉ mikacciṟitu kāṭṭukiṉṟa viyaṉcuṭaroṉ ṟataṉil teruṭṭukiṉṟa cattimikac ciṟitataṉil kōṭit tiṟattiṉilōr ciṟitākum tirucciṟṟam palattē aruṭṭiṟattiṉ naṭikkiṉṟa eṉṉuṭaiya talaivar aruṭperumai evaruraippār aṟiyāyeṉ tōḻi.
translation: Creation is one, smaller than a tiny atom. Smaller than that is the seed of the budding inner faculties. Smaller than that seed is the bewildering Māṉ (the great principle). Smaller than Māṉ is the intellect. Far smaller than the intellect is a vast flame that reveals it. Far smaller than that is the Sakti that brings clarity, and one part in a crore of that is the sacred Chitrambalam, where my Master dances by the power of Grace. Who can speak of the greatness of His Grace? You do not know it, my friend.
commentary: To show how subtle the place of the dance is, Vallalar descends step by step into the infinitesimal: creation smaller than an atom, then the seed of the inner faculties, Māṉ, the intellect, the revealing flame, and the Sakti that brings clarity. The Chitrambalam, the 'small hall,' is one part in a crore of even that, and there his Master dances by the power of Grace. Who could tell the greatness of such Grace?

translit: nāṉmukarkaḷ mikapperiyar āṅkavaril periyar nāraṇarkaḷ maṟṟavariṉnāṭiṉmikap periyar vāṉmukatta uruttirarkaḷ maṟṟavaril periyar mayēccurarkaḷ catācivarkaḷ maṟṟavaril periyar mīṉmukatta vintataṉil peritataṉil nātam mikapperitu paraiataṉil mikapperiyaḷ avaḷiṉ āṉmukattil paramparantāṉ peritataṉil peritāy āṭukiṉṟa cēvaṭiyār aṟivārkāṇ tōḻi.
translation: The Brahmas are very great. Greater than them are the Narayanas. If you consider it, the celestial-faced Rudras are much greater. Greater than them are the Mahesvaras and Sadasivas. Greater than them is the fish-faced Bindu; greater than it is Natham. Very great is Parai, and she is greater than Natham. In the very face of her soul, Paraparam is great. But He who has the sacred feet and dances, being greater even than that, He knows. See, O friend.
commentary: Vallalar lists the greatest beings and principles in the cosmos, creating a ladder of ascending power: from the great gods like Brahma and Narayana, to the point of creation (Bindu), the primal vibration (Natham), the supreme divine power (Parai), and even the ultimate reality beyond all else (Paraparam). He then declares that the one who dances is greater than every single one of them. This asserts the absolute supremacy of the dancing Lord, placing him beyond every other known concept of divinity or cosmic power.

translit: maṇaṉantaṅ kōṭiaḷa vuṭaiyatunīr ataṉil vayaṅkiyanūṟ ṟorukōṭi mēlatikam vaṉṉi eṇṇiyaā yiramayutam kōṭiyiṉmēl ilakkam eṇpattu nāṉkatiṉmēl atikamvaḷi yoṭuvāṉ viṇṇaḷavu mūlamuyir māmāyai kuṭilai vintaḷavu colamuṭiyā tintavakai ellām aṇṇalaṭic ciṟunakattil ciṟṟakattām eṉṟāl avarperumai evaruraippār aṟiyāynī tōḻi.
translation: The earth measures infinite crores of units. Water is greater than that by a measure of one hundred and one crores. Fire is greater still by a measure of eighty-four lakhs over a thousand myriad-crores. The full measure of air, space, Mula-prakriti, the soul, Mahamaya, Kudilai (the coiled primal Sakti), and Bindu cannot be stated. If all these are contained in a tiny part of a small nail on the Lord's foot, who then can declare His greatness? You do not comprehend, O friend.
commentary: Vallalar paints a picture of the universe's staggering scale, from the elements like earth and water to the metaphysical principles of Primal Nature (Mula-prakriti) and the great power of manifestation (Mahamaya). He declares that all of this immeasurable vastness is contained within a tiny speck on a nail of the Lord's foot. This powerful image conveys the infinite greatness of God, who effortlessly contains all of creation within himself.

translit: maṇṇāti aimpūta vakaiiraṇṭiṉ oṉṟu vaṭivuvaṇṇam iyaṟkaioru vālaṇuccat tiyalāyk kaṇṇeṉṉum uṇarccicelāk kāṭciyavāyk niṟpak karutumavaik kuṭpuṟaṅkīḻ mēṟpakkam naṭuvil naṇṇioru mūṉṟaintu nāloṭumūṉ ṟeṭṭāy navamāki mūlattiṉ naviṉṟacattik kellām aṇṇuṟumōr ātāra cattikoṭut tāṭum aṭipperumai yāraṟivār avaraṟivār tōḻi.
translation: Of the two kinds of the five elements beginning with earth, one kind exists as the very nature of a pure atomic sakti, having form and color, yet standing as a sight that the sense of sight cannot perceive. Approaching these subtle elements, pervading their inside, outside, below, above, sides, and center, becoming one, three, five, seven, eight, and nine; for all the Saktis declared in Mula-prakriti, He gives a supporting Sakti close to them and dances. Who knows the greatness of His feet? He Himself knows it, O friend.
commentary: The physical world is made of subtle, atomic energies (saktis) that our senses cannot perceive. God pervades these elemental energies completely, from inside and out, becoming their very substance. For all the powers that arise from Primal Nature (Mula-prakriti), it is He who provides the ultimate "supporting Sakti" that allows them to exist. His dance is the act of providing this fundamental ground for all of reality, a greatness that only He can truly know.

translit: maṇpūta mutaṟcatti vālaṇuvil aṇuvāy matittaataṉ uḷoḷiyāy avvoḷikkuḷ oḷiyāy eṇpūtat tavvoḷikkuḷ ilaṅkuveḷi yāyav viyalveḷikkuḷ oruveḷiyāy iruntaveḷinaṭuvē paṇpūta naṭampuriyum patapperumai evarum pakuttuṇara muṭiyātēl patamalareṉ talaimēl naṇpūṟa vaittaruḷum naṭarājap perumāṉ nallaceyal vallapamār colluvarkāṇ tōḻi.
translation: As an atom within the pure atom of the primary sakti of the earth element; as the light within that esteemed atom, and the light within that light; as the shining space within the light of that noble element, and as a space within that natural space: in the middle of that very space, He performs the dance of His nature. If the greatness of that foot can be comprehended by no one through analysis, then who can speak of the mastery of the good deeds of the great Lord Nataraja, who, with overflowing friendship, graciously placed His flower-foot upon my head? See, O friend.
commentary: God's presence is found by looking deeper and deeper into the heart of matter, like finding a light within a light, or a space within a space. It is in this ultimate, subtle core of reality that the divine dance unfolds. Vallalar then brings this cosmic vision to a deeply personal level: the foot of this immeasurable Lord, Nataraja (Siva, the cosmic dancer), has been placed upon his own head. This is a powerful symbol of grace, showing that the most vast and subtle power in the universe can also offer a direct, intimate blessing.

translit: vaṇkalappil canticeyum cattiyuḷē orumai vayaṅkoḷimā cattiata ṉuḷorukā raṇamām viṇkaraṇa cattiata ṉuḷtalaimai yāka viḷaṅkukuruc cattiatiṉ meymmaivaṭi vāṉa eṇkuṇamā catti intac cattitaṉak kuḷḷē iṟaiyāki atuatuvāy ilaṅkinaṭam puriyum taṇkaruṇait tiruvaṭiyiṉ perumaiaṟi varitēl cāmitiru mēṉiyiṉcīr cāṟṟuvateṉ tōḻi.
translation: Within the Sakti that joins in generous union is the great Sakti of singular, radiant light. Within that is the causal Vinkarana Sakti. Within that, shining pre-eminently, is the Guru Sakti. Within that is the great Sakti of eight qualities, which is the very form of truth. If it is difficult to know the greatness of the cool, merciful, sacred foot that, as Lord within this Sakti, shines as each and every one of these and performs the dance, then how can one describe the glory of the Master's sacred form, O friend?
commentary: God's power, or Sakti, unfolds in layers of increasing subtlety and significance. Vallalar describes a progression: from a general power of creation, to a power of pure light, to a causal power, and finally to the Guru Sakti, the grace that manifests as the spiritual teacher. God is the Lord who dances within each of these layers of reality. The verse suggests that if this active presence of God is so mysterious, His complete being is even more unknowable.

translit: periyaeṉap pukalkiṉṟa pūtavakai ellām pēcukiṉṟa pakutiyilē vīcukiṉṟa ciṟumai uriyaperum pakutiyumap pakutimutal kuṭilai uḷaṅkoḷparai mutalcatti yōkamelām potuvil turiyanaṭam purikiṉṟa cōtimalart tāḷil tōṉṟiyatōr ciṟṟacaivāl tōṉṟukiṉṟa eṉṟāl ariyaperum poruḷāka naṭikkiṉṟa talaivar aruṭperumai eṉaḷavō aṟiyāy eṉtōḻi.
translation: All the types of elements acclaimed as 'great' are just a trifle cast about within the realm of prakṛti.
